spans.assertion: the analysis used data on 106,803 player-referee dyads from four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain) during the 2012-2013 season
the hypothesis was found to be supported
the primary analysis adjusted for games played, player characteristics (height, weight, position), playing style (yellow cards, goals), league country, and referee country implicit/explicit bias
dark-skinned players have a 0.228 percentage-point higher risk of receiving red cards than light-skinned players (95% CI [0.034,0.441], p=0.016)
the secondary estimand showed an adjusted odds ratio of 1.195 (95% CI [1.034,1.383], p=0.016), i.e. 19.5% higher odds for dark-skinned players
the effect was robust to bootstrap resampling (p=0.040)
the effect was particularly pronounced in England (OR=1.391,p=0.011) and Germany (OR=2.053,p<0.001), but not evident in France or Spain
the effect size is modest but meaningful given the ~1.3% base rate of red cards
the point estimate was 0.2281 percentage points (0.00228 probability units)
the 95% CI for the risk difference was [0.0336, 0.4409] percentage points
the two-sided p-value was 0.0162 at α=0.05
the bootstrap p-value was 0.0400 using 500 iterations
dark-skinned players have a 0.228 percentage-point absolute increase in red-card probability, from 1.22% to 1.45%
this represents an 18.7% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline risk
the CI excludes zero and both model-based and bootstrap p-values are significant at α=0.05, providing strong evidence for the hypothesis
the adjusted odds ratio (dark vs light) was 1.1953
the 95% CI for the odds ratio was [1.0335, 1.3826]
the two-sided p-value for the odds ratio was 0.0162
dark-skinned players have 19.5% higher odds of receiving a red card after adjustment
the CI excludes 1.0, confirming statistical significance
the unit of analysis was the player-referee dyad (N=106,803)
the sample contained 1,339 unique players (1,109 light-skinned, 230 dark-skinned)
the sample contained 2,816 unique referees
there were 1,341 red card events
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of any red card received in the dyad
original red card counts were 144,219 dyads with 0 cards, 1,784 with 1 card, 25 with 2 cards
the overall red-card rate was 1.26%
skin tone was rated independently by 2 blind raters on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.92, Spearman ρ=0.86
light skin was defined as an average rating of 0-0.25
89,535 dyads (83.8%) fell in the light-skin group
dark skin was defined as an average rating of 0.75-1.0
17,268 dyads (16.2%) fell in the dark-skin group

spans.note: rationale that the definition captures distribution extremes

spans.assertion: the model included confounders chosen based on theoretical relevance and empirical association
number of games played in the dyad was included as a covariate (mean 3.0, SD 3.6)
height (cm) was included as a covariate (mean 182.2, SD 6.9)
weight (kg) was included as a covariate (mean 76.4, SD 7.2)
position (5 categories) was included as a covariate
yellow cards received was included as a covariate (mean 0.40, SD 0.83)
goals scored was included as a covariate (mean 0.36, SD 1.09)
league country (4 categories) was included as a covariate
referee country-level implicit bias (IAT score) was included as a covariate (mean 0.35, SD 0.16)
referee country-level explicit bias (thermometer score) was included as a covariate (mean 0.40, SD 0.43)
dyads without skin tone ratings were excluded (21,407 dyads, 14.7% of total)
803 additional dyads (0.75% of skin-tone-rated dyads) were excluded via complete case analysis
height was missing for 46 dyads (0.04%)
weight was missing for 686 dyads (0.64%)
implicit/explicit bias data was missing for 117 dyads (0.11%)
the red card rate in excluded cases was 0.37% vs 1.26% in included cases
the lower red card rate among excluded cases likely reflects fewer games/encounters
the two raters' skin-tone scores were averaged into one score
the averaged skin-tone score was dichotomized into light (≤0.25) vs dark (≥0.75)
position was simplified from 12 detailed positions to 5 categories based on playing role
red card counts (0,1,2) were collapsed into a binary any/none indicator
continuous covariates were not transformed and used in their original scale
cluster-robust standard errors were used
standard errors were clustered by referee ID (2,816 clusters)
no sampling weights were applied
all dyads were weighted equally
player or referee fixed effects were not included due to convergence issues with 1,339+2,816 indicators
referee country-level variables (IAT, explicit bias) were used instead to capture referee heterogeneity
league country indicators capture major contextual differences
marginal standardization (g-computation) was the method used to estimate the risk difference
a logistic regression model was fit
two counterfactual datasets were created, setting all dyads to dark skin or to light skin
predicted probability of red card was computed under each counterfactual scenario for the entire sample
the difference in average predicted probabilities was calculated
the confidence interval was obtained via bootstrap with 500 iterations, dyad-level resampling
the bootstrap p-value was calculated as 2 times the proportion of bootstrap samples with opposite sign
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is supported by the data
